earlier_scan.source_named: No grammar or phonology located for Baelelea; Glottolog page shows no descriptive references.

sources.citation: OLAC. Resources in and about the Baelelea language (ISO 639-3 bvc). Internet Archive copy 2024 of language-archives.org/language/bvc.
sources.note: 'Language descriptions' lists only the Glottolog stub. Primary texts are PARADISEC audio only: Capell AC1-433 'Malaita Island (north and south), Guadalcanal Island' (1970) and Ian Frazer's IF01 cassette series 1973-74. No SIL, no thesis, no dictionary entry for bvc.

sources.citation: StressTyp2 v1 database dump (2015-04-14).
sources.note: bvc/Baelelea occurs only in the ISO-639-3 code table; no stress record for the language.

sources.citation: Lichtenberk, Frantisek. 2008. A Grammar of Toqabaqita (Mouton Grammar Library 42). Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. ch. 1.1 p.1 and sect. 2.3 Stress pp.19-27.
sources.note: Baelelea appears only on p.1 as a co-'dialect' of Tryon & Hackman's North Malaitan and in one lexical note (noni 'body' also in Baelelea per T&H 1983). The stress rules of sect. 2.3 are stated for Toqabaqita alone; no claim is made about Baelelea.

sources.citation: Simons, Gary F. [1980]. A survey of reading ability among the To'abaita speakers of Malaita. 'O'O: Journal of Solomon Islands Studies. (SIL Scholars reprint scan, image-only PDF; scanned text.)
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Nothing on phonology at all (reading/writing test methodology and results). The only Baelelea sentence: 'The Matakwalao ward includes To'abaita, Baelelea, and Lau speakers.' The two scanned hits for 'stress' are rhetorical.

sources.citation: Lewis, M. Paul, Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig (eds.). 2016. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 19th edition. Dallas: SIL International. Entry 'Baelelea' [bvc] (Internet Archive copy 2016-08-14); also Gordon (ed.) 2005, 15th edition, same entry (capture 2006-01-04).
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Nothing. 19th ed.: 'Dialects: None known. Baelelea and Baeggu [bvd] almost equal intelligibility of To'abaita [mlu] and Lau [llu]. Typology: SVO.. Language Development: Literacy rate in L1: 30%-60%. Literacy rate in L2: 25%-50%. NT: 2014.. Writing: Latin script [Latn].' 15th ed. (2005): 'Comments: SVO. Mountain slope, coastal..'. No stress, accent or tone remark in either edition, so the list of works to obtain guess that Ethnologue might state stress is closed negatively.

sources.citation: Lichtenberk, Frantisek. 2008. A Dictionary of Toqabaqita (Solomon Islands). Pacific Linguistics 592. Introduction pp.1, 9.
sources.note: p.1: Toqabaqita, Baeguu, Baelelea, Fataleka and Lau 'are considered to be different languages' by speakers though T&H treat them as North Malaitan dialects; p.9: 'With some exceptions stress is predictable' -- Toqabaqita only, nothing about Baelelea.

sources.citation: Wurm, S. A., P. Mühlhäusler & D. T. Tryon (eds.). 1996. Atlas of Languages of Intercultural Communication in the Pacific, Asia, and the Americas (Trends in Linguistics. Documentation 13). Berlin/New York: Mouton de Gruyter. DOI 10.1515/9783110819724. [held page-text, 1903 PDF pages]
sources.note: Data only, no prosody: a pronoun table (from Siegel 1986a: 453) comparing Lau, To'abaita, Baelelea, Baegu, Fataleka with the Fiji settlement koine Wai (1s nau, 2s 'oe, 3s nia, dual koro, trial kolu..). No stress or accent marks, no statement.

sources.citation: Siegel, Jeff. 1986. Wai: a Malaitan language in Fiji. In Geraghty, Carrington & Wurm (eds), FOCAL II, 435-463. Pacific Linguistics C-94.
sources.note: Names Baelelea among the mutually intelligible North Malaitan varieties (p.442) and consulted one Baelelea speaker, Manuel Maesua (note 15, p.459); sec. 3.2 'Wai phonology' (pp.447-448) covers segments and vowel length of Wai, the Fiji koine, only. Nothing on stress for Wai or Baelelea.

sources.citation: Tryon, Darrell T. & B. D. Hackman. 1983. Solomon Islands languages: an internal classification. Pacific Linguistics C-72. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Mbaelelea is wordlist no. 65 (Ma) and a 'major dialect or sublanguage' of North Malaitan with To'ambaita, Mbaengguu, Fataleka (p.27; Lau kept separate 'for reasons of tradition', p.27 fn.1). Wordlists and sound-correspondence tables only; a full-text search for stress/accent/penult finds no statement about stress in any language.

sources.citation: Tryon, D. T. 1982. Towards a classification of Solomon Islands languages. In Amran Halim, Lois Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 1: Currents in Oceanic, 97-108. Pacific Linguistics C-74. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Classification only; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Simons, Gary F. 1980. Morphological reconstruction and change in the pronoun systems of the Malaitan languages. Paper presented at the Third New Zealand Linguistics Conference, Auckland, 3-5 September 1980. Full text on SIL Scholars (gary_f_simons/unpublished/pml_pronouns).
sources.note: Phonology content is segmental/comparative only: Fig. 6 regular consonant correspondences (BLE k k '/0 d r l m n ng s) with the note 'In BLE, BGU, FTK, GUL, LAU, and LNG, *' (glottal stop) becomes ' initially, and drops out medially'; vowel assimilation in pronoun forms. The single token of 'stress' is generic ('morphemes.. occur in unstressed positions'); no statement on Baelelea word stress or tone.

sources.citation: Simons, Gary F. [1977]. Standardized alphabets for Malaitan languages. Working Papers for the Language Variation and Limits to Communication Project, No. 5. Ithaca, NY: Cornell University and Summer Institute of Linguistics. 34 pp. (fieldwork July-August 1977; SIL Scholars reprint scan).
sources.note: First-hand but orthography-oriented: sect. 4.1 five vowels plus contrastive lengthened vowels in 'all Malaitan languages' (macron recommended); sect. 2.2.2 'In To'ambaita, Mbaelelea, Mbaenggu, and Fataleka, these four stops [b d g gw] are pronounced with prenasalization'; sect. 4.2 glottal stop; sect. 4.3.3 'The standardized alphabet for Mbaelelea is equivalent to the To'ambaita alphabet. I am aware of no literature printed in the Mbaelelea language. In the churches, Mbaelelea people have used To'ambaita and Lau publications.' The only stress statement in the paper is for Kwara'ae (David Gege…

sources.citation: Voegelin, C. F. & F. M. Voegelin. 1964. Languages of the World: Indo-Pacific Fascicle Three. Anthropological Linguistics 6(9). (ERIC ED010354; Solomon Islands sections compiled from Capell 1962 and Ivens's BSOS grammars.)
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Listed as part of Dyen's 'Lauic Subfamily' hyphenated with Toqabaita and Baegu; no phonology; no Malaita stress statement anywhere in the fascicle.

sources.citation: Ivens, Walter G. 1930. The Island Builders of the Pacific. London: Seeley, Service & Co. (ch. 'North Mala', pp. 24-28: enumeration of the North Malaita peoples and speech divisions.)
sources.note: Ethnographic enumeration of North Mala speech divisions; Baelelea named as a subdivision of To'oa Baita; the book has no occurrence of stress/accent in a linguistic sense.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3. Languoid page Baelelea (bael1237). Hammarström, Forkel, Haspelmath & Bank (eds).
sources.note: Only two references attached: Tryon & Hackman 1983 (overview/wordlist) and Siegel 1986 (overview); no grammar, sketch, phonology or dictionary; AES 6a vigorous. Nothing on stress.
